Design question: Target architecture
Agreed rule / proposed option: Use existing x86 xv6-public tree (PDF 3).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Adapt project mechanisms to real x86 interfaces; do not copy RISC-V prototypes.

Design question: Meaning of speculation ID
Agreed rule / proposed option: One ID identifies one shared attempt, not a process or a type of speculation.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Participants refer to one shared context holding private state. Exact ID allocation/range remains open.

Design question: Whether nested xbegin() is rejected.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Reject nested xbegin with -1.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Check membership before allocation; retain existing ID and changes; child calling xbegin is also nested. A new begin after a completed speculation is allowed.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Owner is the process that successfully calls xbegin.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Record owner identity in shared context; fork does not transfer ownership.

Design question: Fork inheritance
Agreed rule / proposed option: Children inherit the parent speculation ID.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Register child membership safely; descendants share private filesystem changes and held output.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Only owner may call xcommit successfully.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Non-owner: return -1 without changing speculation. Owner also must be sole remaining participant.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Only owner may call xabort successfully in iteration 1.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Non-owner: return -1 unchanged. Any-member abort is a possible future extension, not current policy.

Design question: How commit waits for or stops other participating processes.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Return -1; do not wait, freeze, or terminate peers for an explicit request.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Check all living participants sharing the ID, including descendants, under synchronization; owner retries after they exit.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Release membership after exit cleanup; retain shared speculative changes/output.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Keep association during relevant resource cleanup; detach afterward. Member termination alone does not cancel the group.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: No longer counts as a living participant after exit cleanup/detachment.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Do not require wait/reaping to release speculation membership.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Kernel automatically cancels the speculation; never auto-commit.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Mark ABORTING; reject new work; mark remaining members killed and wake sleeping members; allow safe exit cleanup; reclaim only after all references/in-flight users are gone.

Design question: Who can commit or abort a shared speculation.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Owner-only syscall permission does not prevent kernel cleanup.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Owner death triggers cancellation independently of xabort permission checks.

Design question: What happens when participating processes exit.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Do not free private state while it is in use; do not make surviving workers non-speculative and let them continue.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Coordinate in-flight operations and exit paths; cancellation is not instantaneous; safe cleanup must remain possible in ABORTING.

Design question: Successful explicit completion
Agreed rule / proposed option: After successful commit/abort, owner becomes non-speculative.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Publish or discard shared state, complete safe cleanup, then detach owner. Failure behavior depends on failure category and needs further specification.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: 8 distinct writable shadow blocks per speculation, including metadata (4096 bytes of block data).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Count the complete modified-block footprint, including inode, directory, bitmap and indirect blocks where applicable. Keep limits in named constants; do not hardcode eight in algorithms.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Commit the entire speculation in one durable filesystem-log transaction; maximum footprint is 8 distinct home blocks initially.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Coordinate log reservation/admission and cache resources; ensure actual commit completion before releasing held output. Ordinary end_op returning does not by itself prove durability when operations share a transaction.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Fail with -1 before the next unsupported mutation; never spill changes to real storage.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Define rollback/preflight for a syscall touching several blocks; earlier private work must remain consistent or mark context abort-only. Exact failure semantics require agreement.

Design question: Maximum shadow capacity and transaction size.
Agreed rule / proposed option: Move to a larger shadow cap with a correspondingly larger filesystem log and buffer cache; exact upgraded sizes remain to be selected.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Upgrade shadow capacity, log space/reservation, and cache headroom together; check log-header capacity and rebuild fs.img. Preserve syscall/lifecycle policies. Rerun capacity, crash and concurrency tests. A 64-block shadow cap is a candidate, not an accepted final size.

Design question: Maximum active speculations and ID allocation
Agreed rule / proposed option: No exact count, ID range or reuse policy agreed.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Choose shared-table bound and safe identity reuse; distinct from per-speculation shadow capacity.

Design question: Conflict rule
Agreed rule / proposed option: First-committer-wins at whole-speculation granularity based on 512-byte original-image validation; losing committer becomes abort-only. Outside writes/unlinks to shadowed blocks/inodes refused with -1 (D20/D33).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Validate every shadowed block against saved original bytes before writing log. Any byte mismatch returns SP_CONFLICT, sets sc->abort_only = 1, and returns -1. No partial publication; staged pipe and console output remain withheld and are discarded on abort/exit.

Design question: exec behavior and inherited resources
Agreed rule / proposed option: No final exec / descriptor membership rules selected.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Define exec association and inherited descriptor handling before broader workloads.

Design question: Console and external-pipe capacity
Agreed rule / proposed option: Console capacity fixed at 4096 bytes (PGSIZE) with short-write semantics; pipe buffering and external-pipe capacity remain open for Step 8.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Choose bounds and failure/backpressure rules; preserve same-speculation pipe communication.

Design question: Failure and crash semantics
Status: DOCUMENTED - STEP 10 (D26, D39, D44, D55, D61)
Agreed rule / proposed option: Atomic file commit; output release follows durability and is not part of the disk log. Crash or kill after the durable point can lose or partially deliver held output; nothing replays it.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Verified by crash points 1-4 (filesystem old/new) and 5-8 (filesystem new; console none or 16-byte prefix; pipe delivery observed). No exactly-once output is claimed.

Design question: Should we reserve shadow-block storage in advance (a fixed pool), or allocate memory only when needed?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Allocate shadow storage dynamically when needed, with a maximum of eight writable shadow blocks per speculation for now.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Keep the limit in a named constant. The context resources pointer refers to the shadow-storage structure; it does not allocate memory itself. Use an extensible layout so a larger cap does not require replacing the storage design. Handle allocation failure and safe cleanup. Raise log/cache limits together before supporting larger commits. Exact page/entry layout will be chosen during implementation.

Design question: How do we stop two members from creating separate private copies of the same block?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Reserve an entry before unlocking. Entries move from FREE (unused) to LOADING (reserved, contents not ready) to READY (safe to access).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Pin the context. Under resource_lock, find an existing entry or reserve one as LOADING; reservations count toward the eight-block cap. Unlock before allocating block storage or reading disk. Relock to finalize READY or release a failed reservation. Coordinate cancellation, wake waiters, and release references safely. Exact page layout and cancellation synchronization remain implementation details.

Design question: Why must we reserve an entry before reading the original block?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Without a reservation, two processes in the same speculation can both think that block 42 has no private copy and create duplicate entries.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Without reservation: A locks, sees no shadow for block 42, unlocks and starts reading disk. B locks, also sees no shadow, unlocks and prepares another copy. With reservation: A marks block 42 LOADING before unlocking. B sees LOADING and waits. A finishes, marks READY and wakes B. B retries and uses the same entry. This prevents duplicate initialization; outside-writer conflicts are a separate later problem.

Design question: Which spinlocks protect the context table and the shadow entries?
Agreed rule / proposed option: ptable.lock protects process membership and context lifecycle metadata. Each context has its own resource_lock to protect private resource bookkeeping, such as shadow-entry lookup, reservation and publication.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Use spec_pin to keep the context alive before using resources, then take resource_lock with ptable.lock released. Release resource_lock before spec_unpin. Do not nest these two spinlocks. Do not hold either across disk I/O or other work that may sleep. A pin protects lifetime; it does not by itself prevent cancellation.

Design question: How should a member wait while another member loads a shadow block?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Wait for a LOADING entry without keeping the resource spinlock held while asleep, then retry the lookup and context checks.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Use the xv6 sleep(channel, lock) handoff or an equivalent synchronized protocol to avoid missed wakeups. sleep releases the supplied lock before sleeping and reacquires it on return. Recheck in a loop after wakeup. Wake waiters on success, allocation failure and cancellation; never expose incomplete data or fall back to a public write. Reading disk does not automatically release an unrelated resource_lock.

Design question: Step 4: What happens when a process outside a speculation writes, truncates or deletes file data that the speculation has privately copied?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Refuse the outside operation with -1 and leave the public file unchanged. The speculation is not affected and continues normally.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Granularity (assistant recommendation adopted with A1): block level for writes - an outside write to a block that any active speculation has a shadow of (READY or LOADING) is refused; writes to other blocks of the same file proceed. File level for freeing - an outside unlink or O_TRUNC of a file of which any active speculation has a shadowed block is refused, so a shadowed block can never be freed and reused by another file. Refusals stop once the speculation commits or aborts. Blocks the speculation only read are not protected (reads are not a snapshot). Two speculations privately writing the same block do not conflict in Step 4; that is a Step 5 commit question. A multi-block outside write refused part-way follows the xv6 short-write convention. Ordinary programs can now get -1 while a speculation runs; this is the accepted cost. Step-4 scoped rule; the final conflict policy O02 remains open. Example: S copies block 42 (Hello -> private World); P's write of Howdy to block 42 returns -1; the public block still says Hello; S continues.

Design question: Step 4: Which open files may a speculating process use for reading and writing regular files?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Only file objects opened by a member of the same speculation, during that speculation. Using a regular-file descriptor opened before xbegin (or by another speculation) returns -1. Console/device descriptors are exempt.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Record the opening speculation ID in struct file at open time; check it in read/write for FD_INODE regular files. Reason: a file object opened before xbegin may be shared with an outside process, and a speculative read/write would move that outsider's offset (a visible effect that survives abort). Children forked after xbegin are members, so they may use the speculation's files. Known cost: files opened before xbegin must be reopened, and shell redirection such as cmd > file gives a pre-opened descriptor that is refused. Per-speculation private offsets are a possible later extension.

Design question: Step 4: What does a speculative write return if it fails part-way (shadow cap reached, out of memory, cancellation)?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Return the number of bytes actually written to the private view; return -1 only if no byte was written. The public file is never changed on any failure path.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Follows the usual xv6/Unix short-write convention. The file offset advances by exactly the bytes written. The speculative path must not hit filewrite's existing short-write panic. The program must check short writes (usually by aborting); a half-updated private view is otherwise possible. No up-front check or rollback is done, because another member can consume free shadow slots concurrently. Step 5 may additionally decide whether a short write makes the speculation abort-only (see R03/O05).

Design question: Step 5: What happens if the owner is killed while xcommit() is running?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Kill wins until publication starts; after that, commit wins. Commit checks for a kill one last time after taking the inode locks and passing validation, just before the first public buffer is changed (the point of no return).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Killed before the point of no return: no public change, the speculation is cancelled (ABORTING) and its private blocks are discarded when the owner exits. Killed after it: commit completes durably and the process then dies on return to user mode; it never sees the 0, but the commit happened and is never described as aborted. Reason: in xv6 a log_write()n buffer joins the shared transaction and cannot be taken back. Cost: a kill during the short publication window cannot stop the commit.

Design question: Step 5: Two speculations privately changed the same block. What happens when they commit?
Agreed rule / proposed option: First committer wins. Each private copy keeps the original bytes it was copied from; at commit, if any public block no longer matches its original, xcommit returns -1 and the speculation becomes abort-only.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Validation and publication run inside one exclusive log transaction with the affected inode locks held; D20 already refuses outside writers, so nothing can change a validated block before it is installed. An abort-only speculation can only xabort (or exit). Step-4 behaviour (two speculations may both privately write a block) is unchanged. Resolves O02 for commit-time conflicts between speculations; broader conflict handling (Step 9) stays open.

Design question: Step 5: Should a partial (short) speculative write make the speculation abort-only? (R03)
Agreed rule / proposed option: No. The program receives the exact byte count (D22) and decides whether to commit what was written.
Action sequence / implementation implica: No abort-only flag is set on short writes. Programs that ignore short write counts may commit a half-updated private view; this is documented. Resolves R03.

Design question: Step 5: What does a crash mean for a speculation that was committing? (part of O05)
Agreed rule / proposed option: Crash before the log header (commit record) reaches disk: recovery yields the complete old file and the speculation is simply gone. Crash after it: recovery yields the complete new file, even if the caller never received xcommit's return value.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Speculation contexts live only in memory and do not survive reboot. The durable point is write_head() of the speculation's own exclusive log transaction. No exactly-once notification to the caller is claimed. Output release (console/pipes, later steps) must wait for this durable point. Other O05 details (output delivery at crash) stay open.

Design question: Step 5: What happens to file offsets of files opened during a speculation after abort?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Leave them as they are. Offsets belong to the members' file objects, not to the public file, and are not rewound on abort.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Documented behaviour, no code. After abort the file contents revert but the offset still reflects the private writes; a program that keeps using such a descriptor must reposition itself (xv6 has no lseek, so reopen).

Design question: Step 6: How do filesystem operations keep private inode metadata from leaking through the shared cache?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Use a reentrant sleeping filesystem gate around filesystem operations and publication; reload cached inode fields for the current speculation/public view.
Action sequence / implementation implica: The gate is held per filesystem operation, not throughout the speculation. Pipes and blocking device reads bypass it. This coarse serialization simplifies directory/inode lock ordering and atomic live publication but reduces concurrency. No spinlock spans disk I/O.

Design question: Step 6: Which blocks count when files grow or names are created/deleted?
Agreed rule / proposed option: All modified data, inode, directory, bitmap and indirect blocks share the same eight-entry shadow limit and one commit transaction.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Filesystem routines use ephemeral private buffers. Normal public blocks remain unchanged until commit. Repeated changes to one block reuse its shadow; namespace operations can fail before eight data blocks because metadata consumes entries.

Design question: Step 6: What happens if creation, deletion or extension runs out of shadow space or memory?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Restore an operation-local savepoint on failed namespace mutation. For extension, restore only the incomplete block chunk and return the completed byte count.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Savepoints are internal rollback records, not nested xbegin. Existing D22/D25 partial-write behavior remains: successfully completed chunks can be committed. Original files remain unchanged. Transient savepoint/candidate pages add memory overhead beyond the attached-shadow cap.

Design question: Step 6: What happens to open handles and the current directory after abort?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Existing-file handles keep their offsets. All aliases of files newly allocated in the aborted attempt are closed. An aborted newly created cwd falls back to root.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Committed new-file handles remain usable. Cache fields are invalidated before ordinary use resumes. Open public handles to a committed-unlinked file retain the contents until final close, following xv6 reference semantics.

Design question: Step 6: What if closing an unlinked private file cannot finish bitmap/inode cleanup?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Restore the failed cleanup and mark the attempt abort-only, because the removed descriptor cannot be restored safely.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Explicit abort/owner death discards the view. This exception applies to final-close cleanup, not ordinary short writes: D25 still allows committing successful write prefixes.

Design question: Step 6: How are public allocation and unlink protected while private metadata exists?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Public allocation skips blocks with shadows and inode blocks reserved by private metadata. Outside unlink also refuses inodes held by speculative descriptors or private inode-block changes.
Action sequence / implementation implica: This conservatively extends D20. Other public metadata changes may proceed and cause full-block original-image validation to reject a later commit. Metadata sharing can therefore cause conflicts between otherwise unrelated files; broader conflict refinement remains Step 9.

Design question: Step 7: Console buffer allocation, capacity, and lifecycle
Agreed rule / proposed option: Lazy single page (4096 bytes via kalloc()) per active speculation context, separate from the 8-block filesystem shadow limit.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Allocated on first speculative console write; freed with kfree() on xabort, owner exit/kill, context reclamation, or post-commit cleanup. Zero memory overhead for speculations that do not write to the console.

Design question: Step 7: Speculative console write interception and filesystem gate bypass
Agreed rule / proposed option: Intercept speculative writes in consolewrite() by checking spec_current(); speculative device writes in filewrite() bypass fs_enter().
Action sequence / implementation implica: All descriptors resolving to major CONSOLE (inherited, dup'd, opened) are caught before physical emission. Non-speculative writes and kernel prints (cprintf, panic) proceed immediately without buffering.

Design question: Step 7: Console buffer overflow, memory exhaustion, and short writes
Agreed rule / proposed option: Adopt Unix short-write convention (D22/D25): write remaining capacity and return count; return -1 if 0 bytes could be written or memory allocation fails.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Never spill unbuffered bytes to UART or CGA screen. Does not mark the speculation abort-only; the user program checks return value and decides.

Design question: Step 7: Durable commit release and unbuffered drain
Agreed rule / proposed option: Drain buffered console output in spec_commit_durable(sc) strictly after shadow_publish() has made filesystem changes durable on disk.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Drains directly via consputc under cons.lock without holding resource_lock or ptable.lock, preventing recursive buffering and lock inversion.

Design question: Step 7: Discard on abort, cancellation, and owner termination
Agreed rule / proposed option: Discard and free console buffer on explicit xabort(), owner kill/exit, or failed commit before durability.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Context-owned console buffer is discarded during spec_complete(0) or spec_reclaim(); held bytes are freed with kfree() and never reach the screen or serial port.

Design question: Step 7: Crash semantics for console delivery (part of O05)
Agreed rule / proposed option: Filesystem durability and physical console delivery are separate effects.
Action sequence / implementation implica: A crash after the log commit header is written preserves filesystem changes on recovery, while console output may be omitted or partially delivered if power fails before/during drain. No distributed atomic delivery is claimed.

Design question: Step 8: Pipe reader/writer membership and visibility barriers
Agreed rule / proposed option: Intra-speculation processes communicate immediately through pipes; external readers (outside or other speculations) receive speculative bytes only after durable commit.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Reader membership dynamically follows open reader descriptors across ptable.proc via pipe_has_external_reader(). Internal-only pipes bypass staging. Ordinary writers (spec == 0) write directly without staging; speculative readers read ordinary bytes immediately without rollback capability.

Design question: Step 8: Private pipe buffer capacity, lifetime, and backpressure
Agreed rule / proposed option: Bounded lazy single page (4096 bytes via kalloc()) per speculation context, separate from filesystem shadows; Unix short writes on overflow.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Speculative writers to external pipes never sleep waiting for external readers, preventing commit deadlock with child-exit rules (D06/D08). Closing pipe descriptors before commit retains pipe reference via p->spec_refs, preventing dangling pointers or premature pipe freeing.

Design question: Step 8: Durable commit release and ordered drain
Agreed rule / proposed option: Held speculative external pipe output drains in spec_commit_durable(sc) strictly after durable filesystem commit and before console drain.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Staged pipe records are drained directly into pipe ring buffers under p->lock without holding sc->resource_lock or filesystem gate fs_enter(), waking sleeping external readers (wakeup(&p->nread)).

Design question: Step 8: Discard on abort, cancellation, and owner termination
Agreed rule / proposed option: All staged external pipe buffers are discarded on abort, owner exit/kill, or commit failure without reaching readers.
Action sequence / implementation implica: spec_pipe_discard(sc) decrements p->spec_refs, wakes readers, reclaims pipe memory if all descriptors closed, and frees the staged buffer via kfree(). Readers observe EOF or broken pipe if all writers are closed.

Design question: Step 8: Crash window and input rollback limits (part of O05)
Agreed rule / proposed option: Documented crash window between durable disk commit and pipe delivery; external input consumption is non-rollbackable.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Reboot recovery restores durable filesystem state from the on-disk log, but in-memory pipe buffers do not survive reboot. Once a speculative process consumes input from an external pipe, an abort cannot un-consume those bytes from the pipe or rollback external writers.

Design question: Step 9: Conflict detection and resolution policy (resolving O02)
Agreed rule / proposed option: First-committer-wins at whole-speculation granularity based on 512-byte original-image validation; losing committer becomes abort-only. Outside writes/unlinks to shadowed blocks/inodes refused with -1 (D20/D33).
Action sequence / implementation implica: Validate every shadowed block against saved original bytes before writing log. Any byte mismatch returns SP_CONFLICT, sets sc->abort_only = 1, and returns -1. No partial publication; staged pipe and console output remain withheld and are discarded on abort/exit.

Design question: Step 9: Supported consistency and isolation contract
Agreed rule / proposed option: Write isolation with first-committer-wins commit validation; non-snapshot reads.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Speculative reads of un-shadowed blocks read live public buffer cache; reads are not snapshot-isolated and no read-set validation or serializability is claimed. Metadata false conflicts occur when different files share a dinode block (8 per block), directory block, or bitmap block.

Design question: Step 9: Synchronization baseline and exit path gate protection
Agreed rule / proposed option: Retain coarse sleeping filesystem gate (fs_enter/fs_leave) as correctness baseline; protect exit() and free_embryo() file/cwd cleanup.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Serializes all filesystem lookups, mutations, view reloads, and commit publication. Wrapping exit and embryo file/cwd cleanup inside fs_enter() prevents races with concurrent inode invalidation and truncation.

Design question: Step 9: Commit completion drain sequence
Agreed rule / proposed option: Drain staged external pipe output strictly before console buffer drain in spec_commit_durable().
Action sequence / implementation implica: Aligns implementation with Decision D42. Guarantees external readers receive pipe messages before console emits completion notice.

Design question: Step 10: Timing source for measurements
Agreed rule / proposed option: User-mode rdtsc cycle counter per attempt (begin / operation / completion / total), converted with a per-boot calibration against host wall time (spbench cal 300 ticks).
Action sequence / implementation implica: xv6 ticks are 10 ms; one attempt is often shorter. CR4.TSD is not set, so user rdtsc works; under QEMU TCG the guest TSC follows the host clock (measured 0.313 ns/cycle, 10.0 ms/tick on every boot). Ticks are used only as a cross-check. CSV lines are written with one write() outside speculation.

Design question: Step 10: Emulator configuration for evidence
Agreed rule / proposed option: QEMU TCG (no KVM), 512 MiB, serial to a pipe (not a terminal). Micro-benchmarks on 1 CPU; concurrency on 1, 2 and 4 CPUs; correctness on 1-4 CPUs.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Absolute numbers are emulator numbers; compare ratios between configurations. Console costs include the emulated UART/CGA output of released bytes.

Design question: Step 10: Original-xv6 baseline
Agreed rule / proposed option: Commit fd7d454 (stock x86 xv6 + course add/hello syscalls) with FSSIZE raised 1000 -> 2000 and the portable spbench (ORIG_XV6). Labelled 'original xv6 (baseline)'.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Modified kernel in ordinary mode is reported separately: it pays the filesystem gate and shadow-index checks, so it is not an original-xv6 baseline. bench/stage.sh orig builds it reproducibly.

Design question: Step 10: Samples and statistics
Agreed rule / proposed option: 50 iterations per point x 5 independent boots (console 20 x 5); iteration 0 per boot is a warm-up reported separately; medians with interquartile ranges; n reported.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Concurrency: 3 boots per CPU count, 20 attempts per process. Raw per-iteration rows kept in micro.csv / conc.csv.

Design question: Step 10: Workloads and failed attempts
Agreed rule / proposed option: getpid; empty speculation; overwrite 0.5-64 KiB; create+write 0-64 KiB; extend 0.5-8 KiB; unlink; console 64-6144 B; outside pipe 64-4000 B; internal pipe 64-512 B; concurrency P=1-8 own file vs same block; memory per attempt.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Attempts that hit a cap (short write) are kept, labelled FAILED with the bytes actually written, drawn with hollow markers, and never averaged into successful timings. The capacity cliff is shown, not cropped.

Design question: Step 10: Resource-use measurement
Agreed rule / proposed option: Measure pages held by one live attempt only in the fault-injection build (ST_FREEPAGES), never during timing runs.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Timings come only from production builds without test hooks.

Design question: Step 10: Additional fault injection and crash points
Agreed rule / proposed option: SHADOW_TEST only: ST_FAIL value selects shadow (0/1), held-console (2) or held-pipe (3) page; ST_FREEPAGES counts free pages; crash points 5-8 in the output-release window.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Point 5 after durable commit, 6 after the first held pipe record, 7 before console release, 8 after 16 console bytes. Harness suite output-crash reboots the same fs.img: new filesystem always; lost/partial output documented, never replayed. Resolves the testing side of O05.

Design question: Step 10: Plotting tool
Agreed rule / proposed option: matplotlib 3.10.7 + numpy 2.5.4 in a virtual environment (bench/requirements.txt); bench/plot.py regenerates every PNG/SVG figure and summary table from raw CSV.
Action sequence / implementation implica: One-time pip install; figures use the validated categorical palette with secondary encodings (marker shape, dash) and failure markers.

Design question: Step 10: Demonstration vehicle
Agreed rule / proposed option: Guest utility specrun (commit | abort | keep PATH; steps as comma-joined single arguments) plus bench/demo.py (20 checked demonstrations) and rule-based agent modes demo speculative / speculative-benign.
Action sequence / implementation implica: The keep guard is a caller-supplied rule evaluated on the private view; the barrier contains effects but does not detect prompt injection. No LLM/API dependency. Command lines must fit xv6 sh's 100-byte buffer and 10-argument limit.

Design question: Step 10: GDB session log (handout requirement)
Agreed rule / proposed option: Record a real GDB session on defect D1 (root-directory hole), before and after the fix: tests/gdb-root-hole.sh.
Action sequence / implementation implica: QEMU halted with a gdb stub; breakpoints on bmap() when root block 1 is unallocated and on fs_finish(). Stock mkfs: hole filled only in the cached inode at boot, re-filled after each abort (entries lost, spectest FAIL). Fixed mkfs: single normal extension via writei/dirlink, spectest PASS. Transcripts in design/evidence/step10/gdb/.

Design question: Step 10: Capacity configuration
Agreed rule / proposed option: Keep NSHADOW=8, MAXOPBLOCKS=10, LOGSIZE=30, NBUF=30 for all Step-10 evidence; R04 stays a planned upgrade.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Every figure is labelled with the configuration.

Design question: Step 10: Defect D1 - root directory size covered an unallocated block
Agreed rule / proposed option: mkfs rounds the root size up to the blocks actually allocated and fails the build if the size covers an unallocated block.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Stock rounding ((off/BSIZE)+1)*BSIZE created a hole with exactly 32 root entries; bmap filled it only in the cached inode (no iupdate), and inode_invalidate() on abort lost every entry in that block. Kernel lazy iupdate unchanged (limitation). Regression: tests/regress-root-hole.sh.

Design question: Step 10: Defect D2 - held output released while holding the filesystem gate
Agreed rule / proposed option: At the durable point only detach held pipe/console output; deliver it after fs_leave() with no gate, inode lock or spinlock held. Order unchanged: durable -> pipe -> console.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Old code slept in the pipe drain holding the gate; an outside reader's console printf (begin_op) then waited for the gate: system-wide hang. xcommit still returns after release, so it waits for a slow outside reader. A kill during release drops the rest (partial delivery). Regression: spfailure drainfull.

Design question: Step 10: Defect D3 - timing-based ordering in spfiletest
Agreed rule / proposed option: Replace the outsider's sleep(2) with a probe that rewrites an original byte of the last copied block until D20 refuses it.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Other older tests still order processes with fixed sleeps (a speculative process cannot signal an outsider without externalizing); none failed in Step-10 runs. Documented as a test limitation.

Design question: Human approval before commit (xask)
Agreed rule / proposed option: The owner may call xask(question) once, only when it is the last member of an active, not abort-only attempt. The kernel freezes the attempt, discards console type-ahead, prints the question directly to the console (the single deliberate exception to the D35 console hold), and reads one line: y/yes -> 1, anything else or EOF -> 0, killed while waiting -> -1. After xask, xcommit succeeds only if the answer was yes.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Freeze is per-process (proc.spec_frozen, cleared on detach): syscall() admits only xcommit, xabort, exit, wait, getpid, sleep and uptime, so no file, console or pipe effect and no fork can change the attempt after the question is shown. The wait holds no spinlock and no filesystem gate. Held console/pipe output is untouched and still released only after durability (D37/D42/D48). specrun ask builds the summary from its own before/after view (sizes only). Tests: spasktest + run-spec-tests.py --suite ask, including yes-then-conflict (case C: a rival commits the same file first; xcommit fails, abort-only, nothing escapes). Case C is ordered without sleeps: the asker reads PIPESIZE+1 bytes from an outside pipe (D44) only after creating its shadow, so the parent's write returns after the shadow exists; the harness types y only after RIVAL_COMMITTED. Disabling commit validation in shadow_publish makes case C fail.

Design question: How do we ensure each yes/no answer goes to the right speculation?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Allow only one approval question at a time. Reserve the console input for that question until its answer is recorded. Other approval requests and ordinary console readers wait. Release the reservation if the owner is killed.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Problem: A asks to delete a file and B asks to create one. A yes meant for B could be taken by A because both read the same input queue. Decision: protect the entire question-and-answer exchange, not just printing. A small spinlock protects ownership; sleeping releases it. Never hold the filesystem gate while waiting for a person. Discard old complete and partially typed input at each question.

Design question: How do we show changes even when a file stays the same size?
Agreed rule / proposed option: The kernel compares every private shadow block with its saved original image. List every changed block, identify file or directory/inode changes where possible, and show escaped before/after byte previews. State the preview limit. Refuse approval if a complete block inventory cannot fit.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Problem: OLD changed to NEW was reported as no changes because the size stayed equal. Decision: compare bytes already stored in each shadow entry; do not copy whole files again. Use one bounded 4 KiB report page. The report uses saved originals, while commit separately compares saved originals with current public blocks to detect conflicts. File previews are limited; console and pipe payloads stay buffered. Owner text is only a label, not the authoritative report.

Design question: Must the owner ask the user before every commit?
Agreed rule / proposed option: Yes. An eligible direct xcommit opens the same user review if the owner has not asked yet. Publication requires an actual yes recorded for the frozen attempt. No, cancellation, report failure or a later conflict cannot publish changes. Only the owner can commit.
Action sequence / implementation implica: Problem: the old commit and keep modes could skip xask. Decision: enforce asked AND approved in the kernel, with no production bypass. Programs may still abort without asking. Test drivers provide explicitly recorded scripted answers; ordinary agent runs ask the human. Benchmarks that include commit now include review overhead and cannot be compared directly with older timings.
